newsitem.title: GERMANY: German chemical sector to post record 1996 results.
newsitem.headline: German chemical sector to post record 1996 results.

text.p: Germany's three largest chemicals and drugs groups are poised to post another set of record profits as a firmer dollar, various divestments and higher pharmaceutical sales offset weaknesses in other areas.

But beneath a glittering surface, analysts see a more complex picture, characterised by Hoechst AG, Bayer AG, and BASF AG battling higher raw materials costs which could not be passed on to customers amid still sluggish economic conditions.
"The currencies will be beneficial to the groups but there were problems in the bulk business, with price weakness," said Tony Cox, analyst at Kleinwort Benson in London.

A softer mark makes German products cheaper abroad, welcome news for the chemical industry after virtually all German companies said the very strong mark helped dent results only one year earlier, in 1995.
But since raw materials are mostly denominated in dollars, companies also faced higher costs.

Hoechst AG and Bayer AG will kick off the reporting season by announcing their core 1996 figures, including dividends, on Tuesday. More detailed information will be offered at Hoechst's news conference on Wednesday, followed by Bayer's news conference Tuesday March 18.
BASF will announce its key figures next Tuesday, followed by a news conference on April 2.

Analysts at six securities houses on Monday said Hoechst, Europe's biggest chemicals group, would post an average 50 percent jump in pre-tax profits, but a three percent drop in sales, reflecting a spate of spinoffs, including the sale of carbon and graphite group SGL Carbon.
Forecasts for pre-tax profit at Hoechst ranged between 6.0 and 6.375 billion marks ($3.7 billion) with predictions for sales ranging between 50.2 and 51.183 billion marks.
"Sales will be down due to spinoffs, but this is also the reason behind very strong pre-tax profits," Peter Blair, analyst at Salomon Brothers in London said.
Hoechst's drugs group Hoechst Marion Roussel again got a high performance rating from analysts but all agreed fibres and plastics fared poorly, with fibres expected to post a loss.

Hoechst's shares have outperformed the German DAX index by 16 percent and the sector by 1.8 percent in the last 12 months and climbed anew late last week amid speculation the group could double its dividend to 2.60 marks.
The group quickly denied the talk and analysts stuck with forecasts for the dividend to be raised to around 1.60 marks.

Special attention will be paid to Hoechst's plans to float certain units, particularly after analysts said they had felt fairly certain of Hoechst's commitment to list HMR this year but now sensed the idea may have fallen out of favour.
"If they move away (from the idea of floating HMR) it will be perceived as being very, very negative unless a better plan is offered," Salomon's Blair said.

For Bayer, traditionally the steadiest and strongest earner, analysts were optimistic across the board, especially after the group's chairman Manfred Schneider already predicted a record profit at the weekend.

Pre-tax profit is expected to rise by an average 8.2 percent with estimates ranging between 4.36 billion and 4.7 billion marks while sales are seen climbing an average 7.6 percent to anywhere between 47 billion and 48.68 billion marks. The dividend is expected to climb 10 pfennigs to 1.60 marks.

Praising the group's pharmaceutical product line, Ingrid Graf, analyst at DG Bank in Frankfurt, said "Bayer has a huge lead over its competitors with its sterling products and lower susceptibility to economic swings."

On the other hand Bayer too suffered in some of its chemicals areas and might take provisions to pay for a $50 million fine for fixing prices for citric acid in the U.S which could lower the bottom line, analysts said.

BASF, which has become a favourite among analysts in recent months, is expected to show a five percent rise in pre-tax profits with estimates lying between 4.30 billion and 4.369 billion marks. Sales are expected to climb about 3.5 percent to somewhere between 47.6 billion and 48.2 billion marks and. And the dividend is likely to rise by 20 pfennigs to 1.60 marks.

At BASF, both the gas and oil business is expected to have performed quite well, helping offset a weaker performance in the plastics sectors, said Christiane Dienhart, analyst at Vereinsbank in Munich.

Looking ahead, analysts expect all groups to present a very favourable outlook for 1997, betting on stronger economic growth, especially as Europe's economy recovers, ongoing benefits from restructurings and the softer mark all improved results.
($ = 1.707 German Marks)
